readerTitle: Thirty freezers, one rival and a month to decide
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (베이커리 카페의 냉동 크루아상, 지역 식료품 체인 입점) · 모든 인물과 수치는 설명용
insight: 출시 타이밍은 한 번의 결정이 아니라 연속된 결정이다. 일찍 들어가되 작게 시작하고, 열성 고객 너머를 확인한 뒤 키우고, 경쟁자에게는 먼저 들어가서 쌓은 것으로 맞선다.
misconception: 먼저 출시하면 이긴다. 혹은 완벽해질 때까지 기다리는 것이 안전하다.

sources.text: Lieberman, M. & Montgomery, D. (1988). First-Mover Advantages. Strategic Management Journal.
Moore, G. (1991). Crossing the Chasm. HarperBusiness.
모든 인물, 매장 수, 판매 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 재구매율 48%(카페 단골)와 14%(기타 고객), 개선 후 27%, 경쟁사 20% 저가, 30개 매장 중 3개로 시작하고 매달 9개씩 확대하는 설정은 모두 이야기 안에서 서로 맞게 정했습니다. 3 + 9 × 3 = 30개로 넉 달째에 30개 매장이 됩니다.
카드에서는 Lieberman & Montgomery와 Moore의 개념만 일반적으로 다루고, 연구 수치나 인용은 쓰지 않았습니다. 출처의 서지 정보(연도, 출판사)를 게시 전에 다시 확인하세요.
8번 카드의 '한 번의 계약이 시장 전체를 가르는 경우에는 속도가 더 중요하다'는 일반적인 조건 설명입니다. 특정 사례를 들지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Thirty freezers, one rival and a month to decide
body: Maya runs two busy bakery-cafés. Her regulars keep asking to take croissants home, so she has developed a frozen, bake-at-home pack.

A regional grocery chain likes it and offers freezer space in 30 stores, starting next month. Her frozen delivery setup is untested. And she has heard a large bakery chain is working on something similar.
You're Maya. Four months, three calls.

image.label: A baker holding a frozen croissant box in front of a grocery freezer
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 앞치마를 두른 베이커가 냉동 크루아상 상자를 들고 마트 냉동고 앞에 서 있음. 뒤쪽 벽에 달력 한 장이 넘어가는 모습. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: The grocer wants an answer this week.
body: The recipe is good. The delivery setup is untested. A rival may be close behind. What do you tell the buyer?

options.text: Take all 30 stores now. Getting there first is what counts.
options.feedback: You claim the shelf first, but untested deliveries to 30 stores can mean thawed, broken packs. A bad first taste is hard to undo, and the rival learns from your mistakes.

options.text: Wait six months and perfect everything first.
options.feedback: A cleaner start, but the freezer space may go to the rival. And while you wait, you learn nothing about real shoppers.

options.text: Start now in the 3 stores nearest your cafés, for 8 weeks.
options.feedback: You enter early without betting everything. Shoppers there already know your name, and you can fix deliveries while volume is small.

cards.title: Say you chose the 3 stores.
body: Deliveries failed twice. Both times you fixed the problem within a day. Then the sales data came in. Who bought a second pack within four weeks?
cards.callout: Your fans love it. Most other shoppers tried it once and moved on.

cards.title: The grocer says: go to all 30 stores.
body: Sales per freezer beat the store average, so the buyer wants to expand now. But most shoppers in the other 27 stores have never heard of your cafés.

options.text: Expand to all 30 stores with the same pack
options.feedback: Your regulars bought on trust in your name. Strangers see a pricey box with no reason to buy twice, so the 14% problem spreads to 27 stores.

options.text: Ask shoppers who didn't return why, fix that, then add stores in waves
options.feedback: You give up a fast rollout. In return, you learn what everyday shoppers need before you meet thousands of them.

options.text: Stay in the 3 stores where it works
options.feedback: Safe and profitable, but small. It also leaves 27 empty freezers for the rival.

cards.title: Say you asked first.
body: The answers were plain. Shoppers didn't know how long to bake the croissants. A box of six felt like too many to try. And nothing on the box said why these beat the store's own brand.

You added a big *18 minutes, no thawing* line, a 4-pack trial size and a photo of your café. Then you opened 9 new stores a month, with Saturday tastings. **Repeat buying among other shoppers rose to 27%.**

image.label: Old box next to a redesigned box with a clear bake time
image.brief: 상자 두 개 비교. 왼쪽은 글씨가 작은 6개입 기존 상자, 오른쪽은 "18 minutes, no thawing"이 크게 적히고 카페 사진이 들어간 4개입 상자. 오른쪽 상자를 강조. 실제 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: The rival arrives.
body: In month four, the big chain launches frozen croissants in 100 stores, priced 20% below yours. Your grocer asks how you'll respond.

options.text: Cut your price to match theirs
options.feedback: The chain buys flour by the truckload, so it can keep cutting longer than you. You'd trade your margin for a fight you're built to lose.

options.text: Lean on what they can't copy quickly: your café name, tastings and a coffee coupon in every box
options.feedback: Your edge was never price. It's the customers and the grocer relationship you built by arriving early and getting it right.

options.text: Pull back to your 3 original stores
options.feedback: You protect your core fans, but you hand the rival the shelf space you spent four months earning.

cards.title: Say you leaned on your strengths.
body: Sales dipped for a few weeks as shoppers tried the cheaper packs. Then many came back. Your repeat buyers knew what they were getting, and the coupons brought new faces into your cafés.
The grocer kept you on the shelf because your packs sold steadily without discounts.
Being first didn't protect Maya. **What she built while she was first** did.

image.label: Two freezer shelves, one with a steady line of returning shoppers
image.brief: 마트 냉동고 두 칸. 한쪽에는 할인 스티커가 붙은 상자들, 다른 쪽에는 베이커리 상자와 그 앞에 다시 찾아온 손님들. 손님 중 한 명은 커피 쿠폰을 들고 있음. 실제 브랜드 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: A small start can become a slow death.
body: Starting small only helps if you act on what you learn and have a clear plan to grow. In some markets, one big contract or shelf goes to whoever signs first. There, waiting can cost you everything.
Early fans can also mislead you. They forgive flaws that strangers won't, so their enthusiasm is a starting signal, not proof.
cards.softwareNote: The same three calls show up with an app. Release to a small group of eager users first. Rework onboarding before chasing mainstream users. Answer a cheaper copycat with what you learned, not with a lower price.

cards.title: Timing isn't one decision. It's a sequence.
body: Each of Maya's calls used a different idea from this unit:
list: **Launch now or wait:** market timing and the beachhead. Enter early, but small, where people already trust you.
**Expand or not:** crossing the chasm. What wins your fans won't automatically win everyone else.
**The rival arrives:** fast followers. Defend with what you've learned and built, not with price.
cards.callout: **Try it today:** for your next launch, write down who your first 50 customers are, and what would make a stranger buy twice.
